extracted.intended_audience: candidates preparing the French agrégation (mathematics) / advanced undergraduate/graduate students preparing oral lessons
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation criteria for preparing and delivering oral lessons for the French agrégation in analysis, topology, functional analysis, and related topics; emphasises what candidates must know, which proofs/applications to present, and pedagogical choices (examples, counterexamples, drawings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the role of completeness for existence theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: Make explicit that one of the essential interests of completeness is to provide existence theorems in infinite dimension, notably in function spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give examples in spaces of functions (e.g., Lp, Banach spaces), show how completeness underlies existence results (Picard/Cauchy-Lipschitz, fixed-point theorems). Emphasise concrete applications rather than purely abstract statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of uniform convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate a good command of uniform convergence and its consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The jury expects solid handling of uniform convergence (examples, counterexamples, use in completeness arguments and in proofs like Fourier transform convergence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough understanding of the Cauchy–Lipschitz (Picard–Lindelöf) theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Know statement, proof ideas, hypotheses, and applications of the Cauchy–Lipschitz theorem; this point is important and often poorly handled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include both local and global versions, linear case, counterexamples when local Lipschitz fails, and applications to existence/uniqueness of ODEs. Be ready to use it as an application of fixed-point theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare counterexamples to show necessity of hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Always prepare counterexamples that illustrate why the hypotheses of a theorem are necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each major theorem presented (inversion, implicit function, fixed-point results, completeness-related theorems, etc.), present one or more counterexamples with sketches/graphs to show failure when hypotheses are dropped.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include meaningful applications (especially to differential equations and analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lessons should include relevant applications, notably to differential equations and to analysis/numerical methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples suggested include pendulum, RLC circuits, Cauchy–Lipschitz applications, Fourier-Plancherel, Dirichlet/D'Alembert–Gauss consequences, PDEs via Fourier series, and numerical methods (Newton, secant, iterative linear solvers). Emphasise how abstract results yield concrete consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain links between iterative methods and local contractiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: When studying fixed-point and iterative numerical methods, make the link between the locally contractant nature of the iterated operator and the derivative / spectral properties at the fixed point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss Newton's method as a fixed-point method and show cases (differential zero) yielding quadratic convergence; relate convergence speed to the derivative or spectral radius. Use examples and discuss conditioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know several formulations/proofs and present multiple approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: For core theorems (e.g., inversion theorem, implicit function theorem), present and be ready to use multiple proof strategies and formulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present reductions (e.g., reduce to 0), fixed-point proofs (TIL via contraction mapping), analytic/holomorphic and Ck versions; explain equivalence of TIL and TFI and show different viewpoints when helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance simple examples and more advanced material
rubrics_metrics.description: The lesson should both dwell on simple illustrative examples and quickly reach more interesting/deeper topics for stronger candidates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with elementary examples to motivate concepts, then move to Fourier-Plancherel, analytic continuation, Hahn–Banach (finite-dimension), spectral consequences, interpolation, etc., as time and audience permit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve deep technical demonstrations for solid candidates
rubrics_metrics.description: Some detailed or technical proofs (e.g., construction of nowhere-differentiable continuous functions, heavy uses of Baire without applications) are intended only for very solid candidates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicate that fully detailed proofs of highly technical constructions may be skipped unless the candidate is very comfortable; prefer to present the idea and applications unless competence is clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't present theorems in isolation—give relevant applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid treating important theorems (e.g., Baire) without presenting a pertinent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you invoke a powerful but abstract theorem, immediately illustrate it with an application (Banach–Steinhaus, open mapping, closed graph, consequences in operator theory).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare and use drawings and geometric intuition when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Use sketches/drawings to illustrate topological and differential-geometric arguments and counterexamples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested uses: Jordan theorem intuition, circle example in implicit function theorem, Runge/Gibbs phenomena, projections in Hilbert spaces, fixed-point theorem visualisations. Drawings help in oral exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know and be able to use key formulas and canonical computations
rubrics_metrics.description: Memorise and be able to deploy standard formulas (orthogonal projection formula, Gram–Schmidt, Fourier/Parseval identities, Lagrange interpolation error, Newton–Cotes orders, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These computational tools are expected to be known and used to justify results or compute examples; being able to derive and apply them quickly is valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish closely related notions precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Make clear distinctions between related concepts (e.g., homeomorphism vs homotopy; algebraic basis vs Hilbert basis; norm-topology vs metric properties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly point out the correct notion for the problem at hand and give contrasting examples to avoid confusion (e.g., spaces homeomorphic vs homotopic, consequences for connectedness by arcs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious with Lp and infinite-dimensional examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Lp spaces are relevant but can be delicate for candidates with fragile knowledge; treat them carefully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Lp examples to illustrate phenomena (completeness, counterexamples, Riesz–Fischer), but avoid overreaching into subtle measure-theoretic pitfalls unless confident.

rubrics_metrics.name: For approximation/interpolation lessons include convergence rates and pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: When covering approximation (Bernstein, Taylor, Lagrange, Chebyshev, Stone–Weierstrass), discuss speed of convergence and known pathologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambitious candidates can give estimates (module of continuity) and show Runge phenomenon; relate approximation to applications like solving PDEs via Fourier series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasise structure and consequences in Hilbert space material
rubrics_metrics.description: In Hilbert-space lessons, distinguish algebraic vs Hilbert bases, know projection properties and criteria for Hilbert bases, and illustrate with examples (Fourier, orthogonal polynomials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Candidates must know the orthogonal projection formula, Gram–Schmidt interpretation, Bessel/Parseval, and be able to discuss adjoints, compact/self-adjoint operator spectra and Lax–Milgram applications for the strong candidate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link abstract theorems to computational/numerical techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Connect theoretical results to numerical methods and algorithmic consequences (e.g., fixed-point theory <-> iterative solvers, spectral radius in convergence of linear solves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present algorithms (Newton, secant, Jacobi, Gauss–Seidel, gradient with optimal step), discuss convergence criteria (ρ(I−A) < 1), dependence on conditioning, and give illustrative calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate regularity remarks and variants (Ck, holomorphic)
rubrics_metrics.description: State regularity hypotheses and their consequences; mention extensions of theorems to Ck and holomorphic settings when relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For TIL/TFI mention Ck and holomorphic versions and regularity preservation of implicit functions (e.g., φ has same regularity as f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about pedagogical choices and roadmap in oral exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Organise the lesson: brainstorm, start with simple examples, indicate what will be omitted, and give a clear roadmap for the oral presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The jury recommends brainstorming to collect relevant fragments, signalling early which deep topics will be covered, and managing time between basic examples and deeper applications (Fourier, Hahn–Banach, interpolation).
